I’ve been in the church choir for, oh, it must be over twenty years now, maybe twenty-five, ever since Pastor Thomas was there, and I used to just love it. I sit in my armchair in the living room, the one by the window, and I just leave the TV on low. I know Martha is probably wondering where I am on Tuesdays, and I know the choir director notices my empty seat in the alto section on Sundays. I know they're waiting for me, but I just sit there looking at the television screen, and I just can't find the energy or the will to get up and put my coat on and go out the door. It's just all gone, that spark I used to have, it's just... missing.

Well, doctor, that’s just the peculiar thing about it all. You’d think I’d be sitting there crying my eyes out, wouldn't you? I don't know if that makes any sense to a doctor like you, but I just don't have a feeling about it one way or the other anymore. Well, doctor, the truth is... I haven't actually forced myself to go recently. Not for weeks now. I know I should, I know my mother would have told me to just put my chin up and march out that door, but... I haven't. The last time I did go to choir, though, it must have been... oh, maybe a month and a half ago? I've known every word since I was a little girl in pigtails. And... nothing. There was no warmth in my chest, no feeling of the spirit moving, no... no joy at all. I just felt tired standing there. I kept looking at the clock at the back of the sanctuary, the one above the double doors, just watching the minute hand move and wondering when I could go back home to my chair. So, no, doctor. Even when I was right there in the middle of it, surrounded by the music and the people I've known for decades... I didn't feel a single ounce of pleasure. It was just... empty. And that's why I haven't been back since. It just takes too much out of me to pretend, when there's nothing real happening inside anymore.

Well, doctor, it's not really tiredness, exactly. I mean, my mother—she worked in the mills, you know, twelve-hour days on her feet, and she'd come home with her ankles swollen up like grapefruits and just collapse into the armchair. I just sit there watching the dust motes and listening to the refrigerator hum, and I don't feel drained of energy, I just... don't use any. Well, doctor, like I was saying... I wouldn't use words like "depressed" or "sad." My sister Margaret, now she was depressed after her husband passed away back in '98. Well, doctor, thinking clearly... I don't know that I'd say I've had any trouble with that. I mean, my mind isn't foggy or anything like that. I remember things just fine. Just yesterday, I remembered that it was my niece Susan's birthday. She turned 42, you know, and she lives all the way out in Omaha now with her husband, the one who sells farm equipment. I remembered it clear as a bell, even remembered she likes those little butterscotch candies I used to send her when she was a girl. 

And as for making decisions... well, there really aren't that many decisions to make when you just sit in your chair all day. I decide when to make a cup of tea, I suppose. I always use the whistling kettle, the copper one my mother left me, because the electric ones just don't get the water to a proper rolling boil, if you ask me. But deciding between Earl Grey or chamomile... it's not a struggle. I just pick one. 

I don't find myself sitting there wringing my hands, unable to choose what to eat or what to wear. I wear my blue housecoat most days anyway, the one with the snap buttons down the front, because it's comfortable and the snaps are easier on my hands than the little buttons on my blouses. So, no, I wouldn't say my thinking is muddled or that I can't concentrate. When I watch the dust motes in the sunlight coming through the window, I can concentrate on them just fine. I watch them drift up and down, catching the light. It's just that I don't have much else I need to focus my mind on these days, you see? My mind is clear, it's just... quiet.

Well, doctor, moving slowly... I wouldn't say I'm moving any slower than I usually do. Well, doctor, choir and quilting... yes, I suppose that's really what brings me in today. It's just like I was saying about the rose bushes. I just don't have the push I used to have for any of it. 

Take the choir, for instance. I've sung alto in the First Methodist choir for, oh, it must be thirty-five years now. Every Thursday evening practice, every Sunday morning service. I used to love the hymns, especially the ones with the big, swelling harmonies. But lately... I just don't care to go. It's not that I dislike the singing, or that I had a falling out with anyone. I know they're waiting for me, but I just sit there looking at the television screen, and I just can't find the energy or the will to get up and put my coat on and go out the door. It's just all gone, that spark I used to have, it's just... missing.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how you’ve been feeling emotionally lately, especially about not having the same interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, that’s just the peculiar thing about it all. You’d think I’d be sitting there crying my eyes out, wouldn't you? You'd think I'd be just sick with worry about missing Martha and the girls, or feeling terrible about letting the choir down after all these years. My mother, Lord rest her soul, she always used to tell me that idle hands make for a heavy heart, and that if you weren't making yourself useful to your neighbors, you'd feel just awful inside. \n\nBut... I don't feel awful. I don't really feel much of anything at all, to tell you the truth. It's just... quiet inside. Like that television I told you about, just a low murmur that doesn't really mean anything. I sit there in my chair, and I know I should care. I know I should be upset that I'm not finishing that quilt—I've got all the fabric cut out in these little pink and white squares sitting in a wicker basket right next to the sofa, just gathering dust. But when I look at the basket, I don't feel sad, and I don't feel happy. I just... look at it. \n\nIt's like the part of me that used to get all excited about things, or even get upset about things, it just packed up and left. I don't know if that makes any sense to a doctor like you, but I just don't have a feeling about it one way or the other anymore. I just sit and watch the dust float in the sunlight coming through the window, and there's just... no feeling there at all.\n\nDoctor: Doctor: You mentioned you don’t feel sad or happy about missing your quilting circle or the choir. Can you tell me if you’ve noticed that you no longer take pleasure in those activities, even when you do manage to do them?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, like I was saying before... it's just that I don't have the push I used to have for any of it. Not for the choir, not for the quilting, not even for visiting folks. Even if I did manage to drag myself out the door—which I don't, I just can't seem to do it—I don't think it would matter. Because what brings me in is exactly that. Most days, I just sit at home in that armchair. I sit there with the TV on low, just flickering away, even though I know people are expecting me. \n\nMartha, she's probably got the coffee on right now, expecting me to walk through her door with my thimble and thread, and Pastor Thomas, well, he always relies on me to have the sheet music sorted. I know they're waiting. But I just sit there. And if I were to go, if I were to somehow get my coat on and walk over to Martha's house and sit down with the girls... I just know I wouldn't feel that spark. That joy I used to get when we'd finish a particularly tricky corner of a quilt, or when the choir finally got the harmony right on 'How Great Thou Art'... it's just not there waiting for me anymore. It's why I just stay in my chair. There's no pull to go, and no reward if I did. It's just... flat. Everything is just flat, and I just don't have the push to do anything about it.\n\nDoctor: When you think about times you may have participated in choir or quilting recently, even if you forced yourself, did you experience any pleasure or enjoyment at all during those moments?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, the truth is... I haven't actually forced myself to go recently. Not for weeks now. I know I should, I know my mother would have told me to just put my chin up and march out that door, but... I haven't. The last time I did go to choir, though, it must have been... oh, maybe a month and a half ago? Yes, it was the first Sunday of the month, because that's when we always do communion, and I always used to make sure the little cups were all lined up straight. \n\nBut even then, when I was standing there in my robe—and it's a lovely robe, you know, we raised the money for new ones three years ago, a deep burgundy color with gold trim—I was standing right there in my usual spot, next to Sarah, and we were singing one of my absolute favorites, 'In the Garden.' I've known every word since I was a little girl in pigtails. And... nothing. I was singing the words, and I could hear Sarah's lovely soprano voice right beside me, but inside... it was just like I was reciting a grocery list. \n\nThere was no warmth in my chest, no feeling of the spirit moving, no... no joy at all. I just felt tired standing there. I kept looking at the clock at the back of the sanctuary, the one above the double doors, just watching the minute hand move and wondering when I could go back home to my chair. So, no, doctor. Even when I was right there in the middle of it, surrounded by the music and the people I've known for decades... I didn't feel a single ounce of pleasure. It was just... empty. And that's why I haven't been back since. It just takes too much out of me to pretend, when there's nothing real happening inside anymore.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt unusually tired or have you noticed a decrease in your energy levels most of the day, nearly every day, over the past two weeks?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it's not really tiredness, exactly. I mean, my mother—she worked in the mills, you know, twelve-hour days on her feet, and she'd come home with her ankles swollen up like grapefruits and just collapse into the armchair. Now, that was tired. She'd be so worn out she couldn't even keep her eyes open through the evening news. But me? I'm not doing any heavy lifting. I'm not scrubbing floors on my hands and knees or running after little ones anymore. \n\nIt's just... I sit in my chair by the window. The one with the floral upholstery that I bought at the Sears Roebuck back in '92. I sit there, and I don't feel sleepy, like I need to take a nap or anything like that. I don't feel like my muscles are aching from exertion. It's just that I don't have the... the will to move. It's not a physical exhaustion, if that makes sense. It's just that everything feels like it would take too much effort, even though I'm not actually tired in my bones. I just sit there watching the dust motes and listening to the refrigerator hum, and I don't feel drained of energy, I just... don't use any. So no, I wouldn't say I'm unusually tired or lacking energy like I've been working hard. I just don't do anything to be tired from.\n\nDoctor: Doctor: Have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, over the past two weeks?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, like I was saying... I wouldn't use words like \"depressed\" or \"sad.\" My sister Margaret, now she was depressed after her husband passed away back in '98. She cried every day for a year, wouldn't eat, just wept and wept until her eyes were swollen shut. That's what I think of when I hear that word. But me? No, I don't feel like crying. I don't feel that heavy, weeping sort of sadness in my chest. \n\nIt's just that flat feeling I mentioned before. I sit in my chair, the floral one, and I just look out the window at Mrs. Higgins' rose bushes next door. I don't feel sad about not asking her, and I don't feel hopeless, like the world is ending or anything dramatic like that. I just feel... nothing at all. \n\nIt's like the volume on my feelings got turned all the way down to zero. I don't feel down in the dumps, I don't feel like giving up on life... I just don't feel much of anything. So if you're asking if I'm sitting around crying or feeling miserable and hopeless all day, every day... no, I'm really not. I'm just sitting there, plain and simple, not feeling sad, not feeling happy, just... sitting.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions lately?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, thinking clearly... I don't know that I'd say I've had any trouble with that. I mean, my mind isn't foggy or anything like that. I remember things just fine. Just yesterday, I remembered that it was my niece Susan's birthday. She turned 42, you know, and she lives all the way out in Omaha now with her husband, the one who sells farm equipment. I remembered it clear as a bell, even remembered she likes those little butterscotch candies I used to send her when she was a girl. \n\nAnd as for making decisions... well, there really aren't that many decisions to make when you just sit in your chair all day. I decide when to make a cup of tea, I suppose. I always use the whistling kettle, the copper one my mother left me, because the electric ones just don't get the water to a proper rolling boil, if you ask me. But deciding between Earl Grey or chamomile... it's not a struggle. I just pick one. \n\nI don't find myself sitting there wringing my hands, unable to choose what to eat or what to wear. I wear my blue housecoat most days anyway, the one with the snap buttons down the front, because it's comfortable and the snaps are easier on my hands than the little buttons on my blouses. So, no, I wouldn't say my thinking is muddled or that I can't concentrate. When I watch the dust motes in the sunlight coming through the window, I can concentrate on them just fine. I watch them drift up and down, catching the light. It's just that I don't have much else I need to focus my mind on these days, you see? My mind is clear, it's just... quiet.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed that you’ve been moving more slowly than usual or, on the other hand, been restless or fidgety lately?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, moving slowly... I wouldn't say I'm moving any slower than I usually do. I mean, I'm 67 years old, so I'm not exactly sprinting around the house like a teenager, but I get up from my floral chair just the same as I always have. When I go to the kitchen to make my tea, the Earl Grey or the chamomile, I walk at my normal pace. I don't feel like I'm wading through molasses or like my legs are made of lead. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, now he moves slowly. He had that hip replacement back in 2015, and he shuffles down the driveway to get his paper every morning, taking a good ten minutes just to reach the mailbox. But me? No, I move just fine when I need to.\n\nAnd as for being restless or fidgety... no, not at all. Like I said, I just sit in my chair by the window. I don't tap my feet, I don't wring my hands, I don't feel like I have ants in my pants, as my mother used to say. I can sit perfectly still for hours, just watching the sunlight move across the carpet or listening to the refrigerator hum. I don't feel that urge to pace the floors or pick at my cuticles. My niece Susan, the one in Omaha, she's a fidgeter. Whenever she visits, she's always bouncing her leg or twisting her rings around her fingers. But I'm quite content to just sit quietly. So, no, I haven't noticed any changes like that—no moving slowly, and certainly no restlessness. I'm just sitting, plain and simple.\n\nDoctor: Have you completely lost interest in activities you used to enjoy, such as choir or quilting, to the point where you no longer care about participating in them at all?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, choir and quilting... yes, I suppose that's really what brings me in today. I've sung alto in the First Methodist choir for, oh, it must be thirty-five years now. Every Thursday evening practice, every Sunday morning service. I used to love the hymns, especially the ones with the big, swelling harmonies. But lately... I just don't care to go. It's not that I dislike the singing, or that I had a falling out with anyone. Mrs. Gable, the choir director, she's a lovely woman, always brings lemon bars to practice. I look at them, and I know I should be piecing them together, but I just don't have the urge. I don't care about finishing it, which is strange for me, because I've always prided myself on my handiwork. \n\nEven visiting folks... Well, yes, like I was just saying a moment ago, doctor, that's really exactly what brings me in today. I just don't have the push I used to have for... well, for anything at all. It's not that I'm sitting there crying or feeling sorry for myself, I just don't have the care in me to do any of those things anymore.

Well, doctor, down... depressed... hopeless... no, I wouldn't use those words at all. It's not like that. I know what depression looks like, believe me. My cousin Martha, she had terrible depression after her husband passed away back in '98. She would sit in her parlor and just weep, day in and day out. I’d be there early to set up the hymnals and everything. And my quilting circle, too. We used to meet every Tuesday morning without fail, rain or shine, over at Martha's house, and we'd work on these beautiful double-wedding-ring patterns and catch up on all the neighborhood news. I used to love visiting folks, too, taking a pie over if someone was under the weather. \n\nBut lately... I just can't seem to make myself do it. It’s like the battery is just completely drained right out of me. What brings me in is that most days, I just sit at home. I sit in my armchair in the living room, the one by the window, and I just leave the TV on low. I don't even really watch it, it's just sort of flickering there with the volume turned down so it's just a murmur. And the worst part is, I know people are expecting me. I know Martha is probably wondering where I am on Tuesdays, and I know the choir director notices my empty seat in the alto section on Sundays. I know they're waiting for me, but I just sit there looking at the television screen, and I just can't find the energy or the will to get up and put my coat on and go out the door. It's just all gone, that spark I used to have, it's just... missing.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how you’ve been feeling emotionally lately, especially about not having the same interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, that’s just the peculiar thing about it all. You’d think I’d be sitting there crying my eyes out, wouldn't you? You'd think I'd be just sick with worry about missing Martha and the girls, or feeling terrible about letting the choir down after all these years. My mother, Lord rest her soul, she always used to tell me that idle hands make for a heavy heart, and that if you weren't making yourself useful to your neighbors, you'd feel just awful inside. \n\nBut... I don't feel awful. I don't really feel much of anything at all, to tell you the truth. It's just... quiet inside. Like that television I told you about, just a low murmur that doesn't really mean anything. I sit there in my chair, and I know I should care. Well, thinking... no, doctor, my mind is just as clear as a bell, it really is. I don't have any trouble with my memory or getting confused, if that's what you're getting at. Why, just the other day, Margaret—I told you about my sister Margaret—she called and was trying to remember the name of that woman who used to run the little bakery down on Elm Street back in the eighties. Margaret was going on and on, saying, 'Oh, you know, she had the bright red hair and that terrible limp,' and I said to her right away, 'Margaret, that was Beverly Higgins, and it wasn't a limp, it was a bad hip from when she fell on the ice outside the post office in '78.' So my memory and my thinking, they're just fine. 

And as for concentrating... well, I can sit in my floral chair and focus on things without any trouble at all. I might just be watching those dust motes, like I said, or looking at the pattern on the wallpaper in the living room. It's a little yellow rose pattern, very delicate, I picked it out myself about fifteen years ago when we had the plaster redone. I can sit there and follow the lines of the green stems up and down the wall for hours without losing my place or forgetting what I'm looking at. My thoughts don't get all jumbled up. It's not like my head is full of cotton or anything like that. 

And making decisions... well, I know exactly what I want and what I should be doing. I know I should be making that Double Wedding Ring quilt for my great-nephew, and I know exactly how the pastel blue pieces are supposed to connect with the yellow ones. I've got the whole pattern mapped out perfectly in my head. I decided on the layout months ago, right down to the binding. So the deciding part isn't the problem at all. 

If you asked me right now what I want for supper, I could make a decision just like that. I could tell you I'd like a slice of meatloaf and some mashed potatoes. It's just that I don't have the push to actually go into the kitchen, get the ground beef out of the icebox, chop the onions—and you have to chop them very fine or they don't cook right, my mother taught me that—and put it all in the pan. The thinking about it, the deciding on it, it's all perfectly clear. It's just the doing that's gone away. So no, my mind is working just fine, doctor, I haven't noticed any trouble with my thinking at all.

I just... look at it. \n\nIt's like the part of me that used to get all excited about things, or even get upset about things, it just packed up and left. I'm just sitting there, plain and simple, not feeling sad, not feeling happy, just... sitting.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions lately?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, thinking clearly... I don't know that I'd say I've had any trouble with that. I mean, my mind isn't foggy or anything like that. I remember things just fine. Just yesterday, I remembered that it was my niece Susan's birthday. She turned 42, you know, and she lives all the way out in Omaha now with her husband, the one who sells farm equipment. I remembered it clear as a bell, even remembered she likes those little butterscotch candies I used to send her when she was a girl. \n\nAnd as for making decisions... well, there really aren't that many decisions to make when you just sit in your chair all day. I decide when to make a cup of tea, I suppose. I always use the whistling kettle, the copper one my mother left me, because the electric ones just don't get the water to a proper rolling boil, if you ask me. But deciding between Earl Grey or chamomile... it's not a struggle. I just pick one. \n\nI don't find myself sitting there wringing my hands, unable to choose what to eat or what to wear. I wear my blue housecoat most days anyway, the one with the snap buttons down the front, because it's comfortable and the snaps are easier on my hands than the little buttons on my blouses. So, no, I wouldn't say my thinking is muddled or that I can't concentrate. When I watch the dust motes in the sunlight coming through the window, I can concentrate on them just fine. I watch them drift up and down, catching the light. It's just that I don't have much else I need to focus my mind on these days, you see? My mind is clear, it's just... quiet.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed that you’ve been moving more slowly than usual or, on the other hand, been restless or fidgety lately?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, moving slowly... I wouldn't say I'm moving any slower than I usually do. I mean, I'm 67 years old, so I'm not exactly sprinting around the house like a teenager, but I get up from my floral chair just the same as I always have. When I go to the kitchen to make my tea, the Earl Grey or the chamomile, I walk at my normal pace. I don't feel like I'm wading through molasses or like my legs are made of lead. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, now he moves slowly. He had that hip replacement back in 2015, and he shuffles down the driveway to get his paper every morning, taking a good ten minutes just to reach the mailbox. But me? No, I move just fine when I need to.\n\nAnd as for being restless or fidgety... no, not at all. Like I said, I just sit in my chair by the window. I don't tap my feet, I don't wring my hands, I don't feel like I have ants in my pants, as my mother used to say. I can sit perfectly still for hours, just watching the sunlight move across the carpet or listening to the refrigerator hum. I don't feel that urge to pace the floors or pick at my cuticles. My niece Susan, the one in Omaha, she's a fidgeter. Whenever she visits, she's always bouncing her leg or twisting her rings around her fingers. But I'm quite content to just sit quietly. So, no, I haven't noticed any changes like that—no moving slowly, and certainly no restlessness. I'm just sitting, plain and simple.\n\nDoctor: Have you completely lost interest in activities you used to enjoy, such as choir or quilting, to the point where you no longer care about participating in them at all?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, choir and quilting... yes, I suppose that's really what brings me in today. It's just like I was saying about the rose bushes. I just don't have the push I used to have for any of it. \n\nTake the choir, for instance. I've sung alto in the First Methodist choir for, oh, it must be thirty-five years now. Every Thursday evening practice, every Sunday morning service. I used to love the hymns, especially the ones with the big, swelling harmonies. But lately... I just don't care to go. It's not that I dislike the singing, or that I had a falling out with anyone. Mrs. Gable, the choir director, she's a lovely woman, always brings lemon bars to practice. But when Thursday evening rolls around, I just look at the clock and think about getting my coat on, and the drive over there... and I just can't find the energy or the desire to do it. \n\nAnd the quilting... I was working on a Double Wedding Ring pattern for my great-nephew, the one who's getting married in June. I had all the fabric pieces cut out, beautiful pastel blues and yellows, and they're just sitting in a basket next to my chair. I look at them, and I know I should be piecing them together, but I just don't have the urge. I don't care about finishing it, which is strange for me, because I've always prided myself on my handiwork. \n\nEven visiting folks... I used to go over to my sister Margaret's house every Tuesday for coffee and a slice of whatever she'd baked. But now, most days I just sit at home in my floral chair. I have the TV on low, not really watching it, just for the background noise, you know? Like the hum of the refrigerator. And I know people are expecting me—Mrs. Gable is probably wondering where her alto is, and Margaret called twice last week asking if I was coming over—but I just sit there. I don't feel guilty about it, I don't feel sad... I just don't have the push to get up and participate in any of it anymore. It's all just... faded away.\n\nDoctor: Doctor: Have you completely lost interest in almost all activities, not just choir or quilting, but even things you used to find meaningful or enjoyable, like visiting your sister or enjoying a cup of tea?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, like I was just saying a moment ago, doctor, that's really exactly what brings me in today. I just don't have the push I used to have for... well, for anything at all. Not the choir, not the quilting, and like I mentioned, not even visiting folks like my sister Margaret. It's just all gone flat. \n\nEven the tea, since you asked about the tea... I know I told you all about my copper kettle, the whistling one my mother left me, but honestly, half the time lately I don't even bother to fill it. I just look at it sitting there on the stove. It feels like too much of a to-do, you know? Turning the knob, waiting for the whistle, getting the mug out, waiting for it to steep... so I just don't. I just drink a glass of tap water or nothing at all. \n\nMost days, I just sit at home in my floral chair. I keep the TV on low—not to watch the programs, mind you, because I couldn't tell you if it's a soap opera or the local news playing—I just leave it mumbling in the background so the house isn't completely silent. It's just a low little murmur. And I know people are expecting me. Margaret will call and say she bought those little almond cookies I usually like, or Mrs. Gable will leave a message about choir practice, and I hear the phone ring right there on the end table, but I just sit there looking at it. I know I should go, I know they're waiting on me, but the push to actually put my shoes on, find my purse, and walk out the front door... it's just completely gone. It's not that I'm sitting there crying or feeling sorry for myself, I just don't have the care in me to do any of those things anymore.\n\nDoctor: Doctor: Have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, over the past two weeks?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, down... depressed... hopeless... no, I wouldn't use those words at all. It's not like that. I know what depression looks like, believe me. My cousin Martha, she had terrible depression after her husband passed away back in '98. She would sit in her parlor and just weep, day in and day out. She'd call me on the telephone, crying so hard she could barely catch her breath, saying she felt like there was a heavy black cloud sitting right on her chest and she just didn't see the point of going on. She stopped eating, lost twenty pounds in a month, and just looked so utterly miserable, like the world was ending. \n\nBut me? No, I don't feel like that. I don't feel sad. I don't sit in my floral chair and cry. I don't feel like there's a black cloud over me, and I certainly don't feel hopeless about the future or anything like that. I just... I don't feel much of anything, really. It's just a blankness. Like I was saying about the choir and the tea and visiting Margaret... it's just that the push is gone. The care is gone. But it's not a sad feeling. It's just flat. \n\nI don't wake up in the morning dreading the day or feeling a heavy weight on my soul. I just wake up, look at the ceiling, and think, well, here's another day, but I just don't have the energy to participate in it. I'll watch the dust motes floating in the sunlight coming through the window blinds—I have those aluminum blinds, you know, the ones that get so dusty if you don't wipe them down every week, which I haven't been doing lately—and I just watch them float. I don't feel despair while I watch them. I'm just sitting there. So no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling down or depressed or hopeless. Just... empty, I suppose. Just sitting.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulty thinking, concentrating, or making decisions lately?\n\nPatient: Well, thinking... no, doctor, my mind is just as clear as a bell, it really is. I don't have any trouble with my memory or getting confused, if that's what you're getting at. Why, just the other day, Margaret—I told you about my sister Margaret—she called and was trying to remember the name of that woman who used to run the little bakery down on Elm Street back in the eighties. Margaret was going on and on, saying, 'Oh, you know, she had the bright red hair and that terrible limp,' and I said to her right away, 'Margaret, that was Beverly Higgins, and it wasn't a limp, it was a bad hip from when she fell on the ice outside the post office in '78.' So my memory and my thinking, they're just fine. \n\nAnd as for concentrating... well, I can sit in my floral chair and focus on things without any trouble at all. I might just be watching those dust motes, like I said, or looking at the pattern on the wallpaper in the living room. It's a little yellow rose pattern, very delicate, I picked it out myself about fifteen years ago when we had the plaster redone. I can sit there and follow the lines of the green stems up and down the wall for hours without losing my place or forgetting what I'm looking at. My thoughts don't get all jumbled up. It's not like my head is full of cotton or anything like that. \n\nAnd making decisions... well, I know exactly what I want and what I should be doing. I know I should be making that Double Wedding Ring quilt for my great-nephew, and I know exactly how the pastel blue pieces are supposed to connect with the yellow ones. I've got the whole pattern mapped out perfectly in my head. I decided on the layout months ago, right down to the binding. So the deciding part isn't the problem at all. \n\nIf you asked me right now what I want for supper, I could make a decision just like that. I could tell you I'd like a slice of meatloaf and some mashed potatoes. It's just that I don't have the push to actually go into the kitchen, get the ground beef out of the icebox, chop the onions—and you have to chop them very fine or they don't cook right, my mother taught me that—and put it all in the pan. The thinking about it, the deciding on it, it's all perfectly clear. It's just the doing that's gone away. Well, doctor, I feel like we might be going around the mulberry bush just a little bit here, because like I was trying to say a minute ago, I haven't actually *done* any of those things in the past two weeks to even know the answer to that.

The one with the floral upholstery that I bought at the Sears Roebuck back in '92. I sit there, and I don't feel sleepy, like I need to take a nap or anything like that. I don't feel like my muscles are aching from exertion. It's just that I don't have the... the will to move. It's not a physical exhaustion, if that makes sense. It's just that everything feels like it would take too much effort, even though I'm not actually tired in my bones. I just sit there watching the dust motes and listening to the refrigerator hum, and I don't feel drained of energy, I just... don't use any. So no, I wouldn't say I'm unusually tired or lacking energy like I've been working hard. I just don't do anything to be tired from.\n\nDoctor: Doctor: Have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, over the past two weeks?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, like I was saying... I wouldn't use words like \"depressed\" or \"sad.\" My sister Margaret, now she was depressed after her husband passed away back in '98. She cried every day for a year, wouldn't eat, just wept and wept until her eyes were swollen shut. That's what I think of when I hear that word. But me? No, I don't feel like crying. I don't feel that heavy, weeping sort of sadness in my chest. \n\nIt's just that flat feeling I mentioned before. I sit in my chair, the floral one, and I just look out the window at Mrs. Higgins' rose bushes next door. She's got those lovely yellow climbers this year, and usually I'd be out there asking her what fertilizer she's using, but now I just watch them and... I don't feel sad about not asking her, and I don't feel hopeless, like the world is ending or anything dramatic like that. I'm just sitting there, plain and simple, not feeling sad, not feeling happy, just... sitting.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions lately?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, thinking clearly... Just yesterday, I remembered that it was my niece Susan's birthday. She turned 42, you know, and she lives all the way out in Omaha now with her husband, the one who sells farm equipment. I remembered it clear as a bell, even remembered she likes those little butterscotch candies I used to send her when she was a girl. \n\nAnd as for making decisions... well, there really aren't that many decisions to make when you just sit in your chair all day. I wear my blue housecoat most days anyway, the one with the snap buttons down the front, because it's comfortable and the snaps are easier on my hands than the little buttons on my blouses. So, no, I wouldn't say my thinking is muddled or that I can't concentrate. When I watch the dust motes in the sunlight coming through the window, I can concentrate on them just fine. I watch them drift up and down, catching the light. It's just that I don't have much else I need to focus my mind on these days, you see? My mind is clear, it's just... quiet.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed that you’ve been moving more slowly than usual or, on the other hand, been restless or fidgety lately?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, moving slowly... I don't feel guilty about it, I don't feel sad... I just don't have the push to get up and participate in any of it anymore. I know I should be making that Double Wedding Ring quilt for my great-nephew, and I know exactly how the pastel blue pieces are supposed to connect with the yellow ones. I've got the whole pattern mapped out perfectly in my head. I decided on the layout months ago, right down to the binding. So the deciding part isn't the problem at all. \n\nIf you asked me right now what I want for supper, I could make a decision just like that. I could tell you I'd like a slice of meatloaf and some mashed potatoes. It's just that I don't have the push to actually go into the kitchen, get the ground beef out of the icebox, chop the onions—and you have to chop them very fine or they don't cook right, my mother taught me that—and put it all in the pan. The thinking about it, the deciding on it, it's all perfectly clear. It's just the doing that's gone away. So no, my mind is working just fine, doctor, I haven't noticed any trouble with my thinking at all.\n\nDoctor: Doctor: You mentioned that you no longer participate in choir or quilting, and that it feels flat when you think about them. Can you tell me, have you found that you no longer feel any pleasure or satisfaction, even when you do engage in activities you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it's a bit hard to answer that because... well, like I was trying to explain just a little bit ago, I really just don't do them at all anymore to even find out. That’s really the whole crux of it, what brings me in today. I just don’t have the push I used to have for the choir, or the quilting, or visiting folks. \n\nI mean, if I actually forced myself to go to choir... well, Mrs. Gable would hand me the sheet music, probably for something like 'How Great Thou Art', which we always do on the third Sunday, and I suppose I'd stand there and sing the notes. Well, bless your heart, doctor, but I do believe we are beating a dead horse here, because I feel like I just answered this exact same question not two minutes ago. Like I was just saying, what brings me in to see you in the first place is that I just don’t have the push I used to have for choir, or my quilting, or visiting folks.
